---
name: dotfiles-worktree-for-edits
description: "Work on a branch in a worktree in the dotfiles repo, never edit the main tree on master directly"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 69b8c513-84e5-4735-ba7c-dccccfba4cba
  modified: 2026-09-27T02:09:50.986Z
---

Do not edit files in `/home/sauyon/devel/dotfiles` directly on `master`. Branch
and work in a worktree, then merge. The user caught me mid-task editing the main
tree and said so bluntly ("why the fuck are you working in the main tree"),
then: "reset main after you fix it".

**Why:** master is the tree `hms` reads, and `hms` refuses on a dirty tree — so
uncommitted edits in the main checkout block applying config, and they sit in the
one place the user expects to be clean. A worktree also keeps the main checkout
usable while work is in progress.

**How to apply:** `git worktree add .drovr/wt/<name> -b <branch> HEAD`, add
`.drovr/wt` to `.git/info/exclude` (not the tracked `.gitignore`), then
`EnterWorktree` into it. Note that master may be **amended** under you while you
work — check `git merge-base --is-ancestor <base> master` before merging, and
replay with `git rebase --onto master <base> <branch>` rather than a plain merge
that would resurrect rewritten commits.

Related: [[push-implies-hms]]
---
name: keep-test-harnesses-in-repo
description: "Commit a test harness into tests/ rather than leaving it in a scratch directory, and don't ask whether to"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: fca421de-8072-4c37-a36d-4dcc70aceecc
  modified: 2026-09-27T07:56:48.146Z
---

When a change is verified by a harness, the harness belongs in `tests/` in the
commit, not in the session's scratch directory. Asked on 2026-09-27 whether to
commit one (and whether to apply with `hms`), the answer was "always do it" —
both were things to do, not to offer.

**Why:** a harness that dies with the session turns "verified, 33 cases" into an
unverifiable claim. It matters most for code that models someone else's logic
(e.g. `hyprlock-faillock` reimplementing pam_faillock's tally windows), where the
comments asserting the model is right are exactly what needs re-checking after an
upstream bump.

**How to apply:** `tests/<thing>.sh`, self-resolving — with no argument it
evaluates and realises the real artifact and tests that, so it runs with no
setup; a path argument tests a given build. Drive the code through override seams
(env vars) so no real failure state has to be provoked. Mention it in README.
Then apply, per [[push-implies-hms]], and do the editing in a worktree per
[[dotfiles-worktree-for-edits]].
---
name: push-implies-hms
description: "In the dotfiles repo, never offer or run a bare `git push` — pushing means running `hms`"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 69b8c513-84e5-4735-ba7c-dccccfba4cba
  modified: 2026-09-27T02:09:41.497Z
---

Never treat `git push` as a step that can stand alone in this repo. If the
change is going to origin, run `hms` — it pushes, waits for the commit's CI run
on `forge.ko.ag`, then switches to the closure CI built. Offering "want me to
push?" as separate from switching was the mistake; the user's words: "god damn
if you push you MUST hms".

**Why:** a pushed-but-not-switched master is a half-applied state. CI builds
every pushed commit, so a push already commits the machine to that closure;
stopping before the switch just leaves the box running old config while origin
says otherwise, and the next `hms` then switches to a commit nobody reviewed as
current.

**How to apply:** when work is committed and ready, run `hms` (background it —
it blocks ten-odd minutes). Never propose `git push` on its own, and never
substitute `home-manager switch`. `hms --local` builds here instead of
downloading CI's build, and is a deliberate choice to state out loud.

Related: [[dotfiles-worktree-for-edits]]

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cases for which hosts get waypipe, the Wayland forwarding proxy in home.nix's
# home.packages.
#
# What is being protected here is a *pair*, and that is the whole point. waypipe
# is not a tool a host uses alone: `waypipe ssh <host> <app>` runs one waypipe
# locally, next to the compositor that will show the window, and a second one on
# the far end, next to the application. Neither half is any use without the
# other, so "which hosts have waypipe" is really "which hosts can be either end
# of a forward", and a gate that drifts to one host is a gate that has silently
# turned the feature off.
#
# Both halves also have to be the SAME waypipe. The 0.10 rewrite (C -> Rust)
# changed the wire format, and waypipe refuses a version mismatch rather than
# degrading -- so the two ends agreeing is a property of them coming from one
# flake.lock, which is exactly what the version case at the end asserts.
#
# The teeth at the end are about the cases themselves: a change that dropped
# waypipe from home.packages altogether would leave every "does not have it"
# case passing, which is the failure mode a gate test is most likely to decay
# into.
#
#   ./tests/waypipe.sh            # tests this checkout
#   ./tests/waypipe.sh /path/to/flake
set -u

FLAKE="${1:-$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)}"
[ -f "$FLAKE/flake.nix" ] || { echo "no flake.nix in: $FLAKE" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "testing $FLAKE"

PKG=waypipe
# The two ends of the forward. Kept as a list here rather than spelled into the
# loop so the "both ends, or neither" case below can count it.
PAIR=(shiori utsuho)

D=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$D"' EXIT
fails=0; n=0

# The package names in one host's profile. `pname or name` because home.packages
# holds a mix -- nixpkgs derivations, this repo's writeShellScriptBin wrappers,
# flake inputs' packages -- and not all of them carry a pname.
#
# nix eval's stderr is noise on a healthy box and the whole story on a broken
# one, so it is held back and printed only on failure. Swallowing it would turn
# a broken checkout into a host that simply "does not have waypipe", which is a
# passing case for four of the six hosts here.
packages_for() { # packages_for <host>
  if ! nix eval --json "$FLAKE#homeConfigurations.$1.config.home.packages" \
    --apply 'ps: builtins.map (p: p.pname or p.name or "?") ps' 2>"$D/err"; then
    echo >&2; echo "nix eval failed for $1's home.packages:" >&2; cat "$D/err" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
}

has_pkg() { # has_pkg <host>
  packages_for "$1" | jq -e --arg p "$PKG" 'any(. == $p)' >/dev/null
}

# The store path of one host's waypipe, so the two ends can be compared. Empty
# if that host has none.
waypipe_drv() { # waypipe_drv <host>
  nix eval --raw "$FLAKE#homeConfigurations.$1.pkgs.$PKG" 2>/dev/null || true
}

check() { # check <desc> <expected: yes|no> <host>
  n=$((n + 1))
  local desc=$1 want=$2 host=$3 got=no
  has_pkg "$host" && got=yes
  if [ "$want" = "$got" ]; then
    echo "ok   $desc"
  else
    echo "FAIL $desc: expected $PKG present=$want, got present=$got"
    fails=$((fails + 1))
  fi
}

# --- the pair ----------------------------------------------------------------
# The laptop with the display and the desktop with the GPU. Each is the other's
# far end, which is why neither one alone would be worth installing.
for host in "${PAIR[@]}"; do
  check "$host (one end of the forward) has $PKG" yes "$host"
done

# --- the hosts outside it ----------------------------------------------------
# Not "cannot run it" -- waypipe would work on any of these. They are not in the
# pair, and the gate exists so the closure carries ffmpeg/vulkan/gbm only where
# something asks for it.
check "setsuna (not in the pair) does not have $PKG" no setsuna
check "fujiwara (headless, not in the pair) does not have $PKG" no fujiwara
check "kyuusaku (headless, not ours) does not have $PKG" no kyuusaku
check "mari (darwin) does not have $PKG" no mari

# --- both ends, or neither ---------------------------------------------------
# The case the pair-shaped gate exists for: half a forward is not a working
# forward, and a one-host gate is the plausible drift.
n=$((n + 1))
present=0
for host in "${PAIR[@]}"; do has_pkg "$host" && present=$((present + 1)); done
if [ "$present" -eq "${#PAIR[@]}" ] || [ "$present" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "ok   the pair is all-or-nothing ($present/${#PAIR[@]} have $PKG)"
else
  echo "FAIL only $present of ${#PAIR[@]} pair hosts have $PKG: half a forward forwards nothing"
  fails=$((fails + 1))
fi

# --- the two ends agree ------------------------------------------------------
# waypipe rejects a wire-version mismatch outright. Same flake.lock, same
# x86_64-linux, so the two store paths must be identical; if they ever diverge
# the forward fails at connect time with a version error, not at build time.
n=$((n + 1))
a=$(waypipe_drv "${PAIR[0]}"); b=$(waypipe_drv "${PAIR[1]}")
if [ -n "$a" ] && [ "$a" = "$b" ]; then
  echo "ok   both ends are the same $PKG ($(basename "$a"))"
else
  echo "FAIL the two ends differ: ${PAIR[0]}=${a:-<none>} ${PAIR[1]}=${b:-<none>}"
  fails=$((fails + 1))
fi

# --- the teeth ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Both directions have to be represented, or the suite passes having checked
# nothing. Without the first, waypipe removed from home.nix entirely is a green
# run; without the second, waypipe handed to every host is a green run the other
# way.
n=$((n + 1))
if has_pkg shiori; then
  echo "ok   at least one host still has $PKG (cases are not vacuous)"
else
  echo "FAIL no host has $PKG: every 'does not have it' case above is vacuous"
  fails=$((fails + 1))
fi

n=$((n + 1))
if has_pkg mari; then
  echo "FAIL every host has $PKG: the host gate is gone, not merely wrong"
  fails=$((fails + 1))
else
  echo "ok   at least one host still lacks $PKG (the gate is doing something)"
fi

echo
if [ "$fails" -eq 0 ]; then echo "all $n passed"; else echo "$fails of $n failed"; fi
exit $((fails > 0))
EOF
chmod +x tests/waypipe.sh && echo written

# Code Review

## Overview

**They find, you fix.** Follow the spirit, not the letter: dispatching a
reviewer satisfies the letter; one that read an empty diff, or that you never
waited for, looked at nothing and found nothing. The rule is that
somebody who did not write the change has said what is wrong with it — and that
cannot be you. You read the change you meant to make, not the one on disk.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** A finding you settled in your head is one they meet as a bug,
with nothing saying anyone saw it.

## The Iron Law

```
NO CHANGE IS DONE UNTIL A READ-ONLY REVIEWER HAS SEEN IT AND
EVERY CRITICAL AND IMPORTANT FINDING IS RESOLVED OR RECORDED AS DEFERRED.
```

**Read-only** is a trust boundary, not a performance note: the reviewer reads
anything, runs read-only checks, and writes nothing — not source, not git, not
run state. You stay the single writer.

No exceptions. The first names its addressee; the rest hold for anyone.

- **Never run a reviewer in the background — you, the agent in a herdr pane,
  where ending a turn *is* how you report done.** Do not set
  `run_in_background`, do not yield, and do not schedule a wakeup while one is
  out. A backgrounded reviewer parks you mid-turn, indistinguishable from a
  finished turn, and the run stalls until a human nudges the pane. Dispatch it
  blocking and read its verdict in the turn you dispatched it. That reason is
  role-specific, so there is exactly one role it does not bind: the **driver**,
  which backgrounds the panel and ends the turn because its harness re-invokes
  it on process exit — `skills/pipeline/SKILL.md` says so at its own loop. A
  split by role, not a preference. In a pane, the prohibition is yours.
- **Do not judge a change too small to review.** A one-line edit to a condition
  is the size this skill exists for. Dispatch a reviewer over it.
- **Do not count your own read as the review.** Re-reading your diff tells you
  it matches what you intended — the one thing never in doubt. Dispatch someone
  who does not know it.
- **Do not leave it for the pipeline's review phase.** That phase reads what you
  hand it, after later work is built on it. Dispatch here, while the change is
  one commit wide.
- **Do not close a finding by disagreeing with it.** When you will not fix one,
  quote it and write the reason in the report or handoff. An unrecorded
  decision reads downstream like an unread finding.
- **Do not repeat a verdict you have not read.** Open the file the reviewer
  names, or re-run the review when it named none. A reviewer that never came
  back has not said "clean".

## Announce

Say this out loud before dispatching anything:

```
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each change you review, not once for the session.

1. **Write down the change and the exact range** — the files, and `<base>..HEAD`.
   Get it wrong and the reviewer reports clean on nothing.
2. **Dispatch read-only reviewers, blocking, one per angle:** run
   `drovr code-review run <run> <task>` (`<base>` from `<task>-base.sha`, recorded
   before your first edit) — or, **inline** with no run,
   `drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" <task>`. Nothing
   else, and never invent a run to get one.

   It spawns one reviewer per **configured** angle — `config.angles`, which
   defaults to correctness, security, error-handling, type-design — each writing
   `<task>-review-<angle>.json`, merged into `<task>-review.json`. **Read the
   config, not this page**, and cover any lens it omits yourself.

   Tell each reviewer to review as a skeptic, not the author; to say whether the
   tests exercise the behaviour, not just that they pass; to rate every finding
   **Critical, Important or nit** — what the Iron Law gates on — and say so when
   it found none; and to write them to a path you name, so step 3 has something
   to open. The lenses to cover:
   - **Spec compliance** — what was agreed, no more, no less?
   - **Correctness** — real bugs, unhandled cases, broken invariants.
   - **Verification** — do the claimed tests exist, and would they fail on a
     regression?
   - **Quality** — reuse, simplification, consistency with the code around it.
3. **Wait for every reviewer, then read what each wrote.** Open the findings
   file by path, then classify the round by how the panel exited:

   | Exit | What it means |
   |---|---|
   | 0 | clean — a real range was reviewed, nothing blocking |
   | 3 | blocking findings; go to step 5 |
   | 2 | timeout — reviewers are slow, not broken. Re-run the same command: it resumes the panel in flight |
   | 1 | error, or an empty `<base>..HEAD` it refused. Fix the range or the setup; never re-run blindly |
   | 137/143 | **your own harness killed it.** drovr produced no verdict at all, and none of the rows above describes the run. Re-run to resume, and record the round as **unclassifiable** — never as a timeout |

   A reviewer that returned no verdict is none of the five: re-dispatch rather
   than report its silence.

   **Only 0 is clean, and one clean round does not end the loop.** Stop at
   whichever of three comes first:
   - **Two consecutive clean rounds over an unchanged HEAD.** Any edit between
     them resets the count — the second round is evidence about the first only
     if it read the same code.
   - **A cap of six rounds**, which is *not* a clean ending: write up every
     round's verdict and everything still open (step 5), and finish on that
     record rather than on a verdict. Only rounds that delivered every
     configured angle count toward the cap — a missing angle is a Critical
     stand-in, so a round that lost a reviewer never measured the code.
   - **Two consecutive rounds that lost a dimension** — its own outcome,
     neither clean nor the cap: the panel is failing to deliver and further
     rounds are not measuring the code. Name the angles that never ran. Without
     this the loop cannot end at all, since such a round is never clean and
     never counts toward the cap.

   Three caveats the rule owes you. Two cleans make a false clean **less
   likely**, not unlikely, and prove nothing about convergence — in forge#88's
   own data two consecutive cleans preceded a `changes` round with seven
   findings. **Six is a starting number, revisable on evidence**, not a
   principled constant. And every word of this is prose nothing enforces — the
   shape of the *"re-run it"* that produced 47 re-arms over 14 hours.
4. **Check what the reviewer actually read — range *and* working tree.** The
   range must be the whole of `<base>..HEAD`, every file you touched, not a
   subset you picked; **and uncommitted work is in scope, not exempt** — drovr's
   panel reviews the diff *plus the current working tree*. A verdict covers what
   is on disk only if the reviewer saw both. Clean on an empty range, a subset,
   or a tree with unreviewed edits in it is about a change nobody read.
5. **Resolve every Critical and Important finding, or record the deferral with
   `drovr code-review defer`.** Per finding: quote it, then name the edit
   answering it by file — or, if you are not making it, run

   ```
   drovr code-review defer <RUN> <TASK> --file <path> [--line <n>] \
     --severity <critical|important|nit> --summary "<the finding>" \
     --reason "<why it is not being fixed>"
   ```

   A deferral written only in prose is one the next round cannot read, so it
   re-raises the finding you already ruled on. The command appends to a
   per-task log every later seed carries; prose does not.
6. **Re-run the checks after your last review-driven edit, then say it is
   done.** The fixes are new, unverified code: run the tests. When the change is
   not code and has no suite, name what you re-read instead and why it covers the
   edits — written down, never assumed. Report the findings, the edits and the
   deferrals; inside a drovr phase this also gates `drovr phase done`. **Done is
   step 3's termination rule met, not the first exit 0** — say which of the
   three ended it, and on the cap or a lost dimension say plainly that the loop
   ended on a record rather than on a clean verdict.

## Requirements

The middle column is what the claim takes; the right is what gets accepted
instead.

| The claim | Required evidence | NOT sufficient |
|---|---|---|
| *"This change has been reviewed"* | A read-only reviewer dispatched over this change in the foreground, returned in this turn, and the range you handed it, written down | Your own re-read · a reviewer launched and not waited for · a review of the tree before your last edit |
| *"The reviewer found nothing"* | The findings file it wrote, opened by path and read by you — or the review re-run by you when it wrote none — **and** what it read shown to be the whole of `<base>..HEAD` **plus your working tree** | Its summary, however much output it pastes · exit 1 or 2 · a subset of your files · uncommitted edits nobody looked at · a verdict that never arrived |
| *"Every Critical and Important finding is resolved"* | Each quoted, the edit answering it named by file, and step 6's checks re-run after the last edit | A count · agreeing with one in prose · fixing the Criticals and leaving the Importants |
| *"That finding does not apply here"* | The finding quoted, and the reason written where the next agent reads it | Deciding it in your head · *"out of scope"* with no scope named · silence, which downstream reads as resolved |

## Red flags — STOP

Some are thoughts, some are things you have just written. Either way you are at
the line.

- *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* · *"The lead said just
  send it."* · *"It is a two-line change."* · *"I already reviewed it myself."*
  · *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* — each opens a row in
  *Rationalizations*, verbatim. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are about to launch a reviewer in the background and keep working.* →
  Dispatch it blocking. No version of that ends with you reading its verdict
  this turn.
- *A reviewer has not come back and you are writing the report.* → Block on it.
  Silence is not a pass; a parked reviewer is not a finished one.
- *The panel came back clean in seconds on a large diff.* → Check what it read.
  Clean and empty look identical from here.
- **Anything that treats the change as finished** — any wording at all, and
  also committing, opening a PR, or starting the next task — while a reviewer is
  unread, unreturned, or holding an unresolved Critical or Important finding. If
  you cannot name the reviewer and point at what it wrote, change what you
  dispatched, not how you word it.

## Rationalizations

The right column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* | Dispatch the reviewer first, then send it. Two different reads: theirs is for fit, the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant — reading a document aloud catches prose gaps, not retry semantics. |
| *"The lead said just send it."* | Send it after the review, and tell them the call moves. That is a scheduling reflex, not anyone weighing the technical risk — the calendar is theirs, the correctness yours. |
| *"It is a two-line change."* | Dispatch a reviewer over the two lines. Size is not a risk measure, and the risk you estimate in order to skip the review is what it would have told you. |
| *"I already reviewed it myself."* | Dispatch one that did not write it. Your read confirms the diff matches your intent; the defects worth catching are in what you did not think of. |
| *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* | Dispatch here, now. That phase reads what you hand it, after later tasks built on it; a finding costs more at every step it survives. |
| *"The reviewer came back with no findings."* | Open the file it named, and check it read your whole change, working tree included. An empty range comes back clean from every angle at once. |

## Worked example

One read away, in `skills/code-review/worked-example.md`: a 320-line spec, a
client call in 19 minutes, a $45,000 sign-off and a lead writing *"just send
it"* — the rationalization refused, the panel run, two Importants found, the
call moved 22 minutes. Worth reading once; the rules above do not depend on it.

## Cross-refs

- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you repeat a
  verdict: a reviewer's report is a claim, not evidence.
- `drovr:systematic-debugging` — REQUIRED when a finding is a bug: it is a
  report, not a diagnosis. Reproduce before you fix.
- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED when a finding needs new behaviour: the fix is new code
  and gets a failing test.
- `drovr:handoff` — REQUIRED at a phase boundary: deferred findings travel in the
  handoff or not at all.
- `drovr:pipeline` — the driver's side of both split rules: it backgrounds the
  panel, and it runs step 3's termination rule from the loop's end.

Merge branch 'hyprlock-pending-race'

---8<---
hyprlock: patch the race that freezes the lock screen clock

The clock on the lock screen stops a few seconds after locking and stays
stopped. Unlocking at 12:02 today showed 05:12 -- the time the screen locked --
and hyprlock had logged "Trying to update label, but a resource is still
pending! Skipping update." 29,532 times across the 6h50m in between.

Mechanism, in hyprlock 0.9.6 src/renderer/AsyncResourceManager.cpp:

  void CAsyncResourceManager::enqueue(...) {
      m_gatherer.enqueue(resource);   // first line: worker renders and emits
      ...
      resource->m_events.finished.listenStatic(...);   // last line: too late
  }

The gatherer is a single worker that wakes on enqueue, calls render() and emits
`finished` straight away. Every one of our labels runs a command that returns in
milliseconds, so the emit routinely lands before the main thread reaches
listenStatic() -- and an emit with no listener is dropped, not queued. Nothing
then schedules onResourceFinished() for that id, the widget's onAssetUpdate()
never runs, and CLabel::m_pendingResource stays true forever. Every later tick
of that label takes the early return at the top of CLabel::onTimerUpdate() and
logs the warning above.

Being a race, it bites per request rather than at startup, which is why the
clock (update:1000) and the faillock label (update:5000) both wedged on that run
while the date label (update:60000) did not, and why the two locks earlier the
same morning look clean in the journal -- both were PrepareForSleep locks that
suspended immediately, so no timer ever ran.

The patch registers the listener, and records the resource in m_resources that
onResourceFinished() looks the id up in, before handing it to the gatherer.
There is no symmetric hazard: the callback only schedules a 0ms timer, which the
main thread cannot process until it has returned from enqueue().

Upstream is hyprwm/hyprlock#1071, open, affecting 0.9.5, 0.9.6 and main; the
reorder here is the fix that report proposes. A workaround we carry needs
something that says when to stop carrying it, because a patch that has silently
become a no-op still applies and still builds -- so tests/hyprlock-pending-race.sh
reads the hyprlock source nixpkgs pins and case 1 fails the day upstream does
this itself, naming the three things to delete. The other four cases cover the
patch applying under the same `patch -p1` the build uses, both statements ending
up on the right side of the handoff, and the patch actually being listed in
pkgs.hyprlock rather than merely existing on disk.

Verified: 5/5 new cases, 35/35 hyprlock-faillock, all six host configs evaluate,
and pkgs.hyprlock builds with both patches applied.

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF' && git log --oneline -1
home: install waypipe on the shiori/utsuho forwarding pair

waypipe is the Wayland answer to `ssh -X`: `waypipe ssh utsuho <app>` starts the
application on the far host and renders its surfaces here, over the ssh channel.
Nothing in the profile did this before -- pkgs.xauth and X forwarding cover X11
clients only, and a Wayland-native application over plain ssh has no display to
connect to at all.

Gated on a two-host list rather than isDesktop, because waypipe is never
installed for a host, it is installed for a *pair*. The invocation starts two
waypipes: one beside the compositor that will show the window, one beside the
application. Neither half is any use alone, which is what the gate has to encode
-- shiori (the laptop that is present) and utsuho (the amd desktop worth
reaching for) are the two ends that have a reason to forward. setsuna and mari
would run it perfectly well and have nothing to point it at, and it is not free:
this build links ffmpeg, vulkan-loader and mesa's gbm so DMABUF and `--video`
work, so the closure grows on every host the package lands on.

The pair shape is the thing worth testing, so tests/waypipe.sh asserts it rather
than mere presence. Two cases are about drift a presence check would miss: that
the pair is all-or-nothing (half a forward forwards nothing, and a gate narrowed
to one host is the plausible edit), and that the two ends resolve to the *same*
store path -- the 0.10 rewrite (C -> Rust) changed the wire format and waypipe
refuses a version mismatch rather than negotiating down, so "both have waypipe"
is not the property that makes a forward work, "both have this waypipe" is. It
holds because both hosts are x86_64-linux out of one flake.lock; the case exists
so it fails loudly if that ever stops being true. The teeth at the end are the
same two the aur-helper suite carries, for the same reason: without them,
waypipe deleted outright and waypipe given to everyone are both green runs.

One non-obvious dependency, recorded in the comment because the symptom points
at the wrong place: `waypipe ssh` resolves `waypipe` on the far end through the
non-interactive `$SHELL -c` sshd hands it, which reads .zshenv and never .zshrc
-- the same constraint the MOSH_SERVER_NETWORK_TMOUT note in zsh.nix describes.
It resolves because home-manager sources hm-session-vars.sh from .zshenv under
`if [[ ! -o login ]]`, and that file puts ~/.nix-profile/bin first on PATH
(checked in the generated .zshenv on shiori, line 1 and line 3).

Verified: 10/10 new cases, red first (2 pair cases failing on the absent
package, plus the vacuity tooth), 8/8 aur-helper unchanged, and both
shiori's and utsuho's activationPackage evaluate with waypipe-0.11.0 in the
closure. utsuho is not reachable from here to switch -- tailscale is logged out
on shiori -- so that host picks this up on its own next run.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
